title: Mini‑workload scaling primer and repeatability notes
content:
Purpose
This note collects practical heuristics and a small, repeatable harness pattern for throughput experiments focused on "mini" workloads — short sequences, tight token counts, and client concurrency sweeps. Goal: make small-scale experiments (30–300 qps target) reproducible across GPUs and config variants so we can iterate quickly on batching/priming patches without running full long-run benchmarks.

Context and motivation
- Full benchmark runs (hours, many clients) are expensive; we need a cheap, high‑signal loop for regressions and micro-optimizations.
- Mini workloads reveal different bottlenecks: scheduler wakeups, KV-cache priming TTLs, small-batch kernel overhead, and client pacing sensitivity.
- This doc describes a repeatability checklist, a warmup recipe, recommended loadgen configs, and troubleshooting signals.

Summary of recommended approach
1) Deterministic seeds: always run at least three seeds per config (seed 1, seed 2, seed 42) and record RNG + client timestamps.
2) Two-tier warmup: quick micro‑primer then sustained steady primer.
3) Snapshot/rehydration: capture backend primed state after a canonical priming profile to enable fast replays.
4) Observability checklist: GPU occupancy, KV cache hit rate, backend p50/p99 token latency, host CPU, and clock stability.
5) Statistical consistency: require p95/p99 within ±10% across seeds before comparing configs.

Loadgen config patterns (examples)
- Workload intent: short completions (8–32 tokens), typical seq length 64 token context. Use a mix: 70% short (8–16), 20% medium (32), 10% long (64).
- Arrival process: Poisson (exponential interarrival) for realistic jitter; use deterministic jitter seeds when repeating.
- Client concurrency: sweep nominal concurrency = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} per GPU worker to map microburst sensitivity.
- Tokenization: pre-tokenize payloads and fix weights to avoid runtime tokenizer variance.

Example loadgen YAML (mini-scale)
# minimal, intentionally explicit
name: mini-scale-try
target_qps: 150
seq_distribution:
  - weight: 70
    tokens: 12
  - weight: 20
    tokens: 32
  - weight: 10
    tokens: 64
arrival_process: poisson
concurrency_sweep: [1,2,4,8]
seed_list: [101,102,103]
timeouts:
  response: 30s
  connect: 5s
metrics:
  - latency_histogram
  - gpu_occupancy
  - kv_cache_hit_rate
  - host_cpu_pct

Warmup / priming recipe
- Phase A (micro prime): 60s at 1.5× target_qps with minimal concurrency. Purpose: wake kernels, warm page tables, init JIT/compilation caches.
- Phase B (steady prime): 5–10 minutes at 2–3× target_qps with the same sequence mix and concurrency sweep. Purpose: establish steady KV cache hit-rate and thermal baseline.
- Cool‑down / snapshot: capture a priming snapshot (backend state, cache digests, RNG seeds). Use this to rehydrate later runs instead of repeating long warmups.
- Validation: after warmup, check that 5m rolling averages of GPU occupancy and p95 latency are stable (change < 5% in last 2 minutes).

Command examples (internal tooling)
# run full mini-scale with snapshotting
./loadbench run --config configs/mini-scale.yaml --seed 101 --warmup snapshot/mini-prime.snp --record-metrics /tmp/mini-101.json
# rehydrate from snapshot (fast path)
./loadbench run --config configs/mini-scale.yaml --rehydrate snapshot/mini-prime.snp --seed 103 --timeout 15m

Repeatability checklist (must pass for a run to be considered valid)
- same docker image and model version across runs (image sha recorded).
- kernel / CUDA driver and MIG config identical.
- CPU governor set to performance, clocks pinned if possible.
- collect: nvml GPU frequency log, nsys traces for a sample 10s window, OS perf counters for 60s window.
- run at least three seeds; compare p95 and p99 across seeds. If p99 variance > 15% investigate noise sources.

Key observability signals and how to interpret them
- Low GPU occupancy + high p99: likely batching inefficiency or serialization at host side. Look at batching logs and batch size distribution.
- High occupancy + rising p50: kernel-level slowdown (quantization path or memory pressure). Check memory allocs, paging, and quantized kernel paths.
- KV cache miss storms shortly after warmup: priming distribution mismatch (priming set too small or sampling skew). Increase steady prime breadth.
- Step changes in latency correlated with GPU VRM temp spikes: thermal throttling — move runs to cooler rack or increase warmup buffer.

Statistical comparisons (short guidance)
- Use the three-seed set to compute median p95; require 95% bootstrap CI non-overlapping for a confident regression.
- For quick triage use median-of-seeds p95 and require at least 8% difference to label a change as suspicious.

Troubleshooting notes / gotchas
- Clock drift: host clocks can desynchronize between clients and collector; prefer server-side timestamps for latency calculations.
- Background work: other tenants on shared host can introduce jitter. Use dedicated capacity or MIG isolates for reproducible microbenchmarks.
- Small-batch noise: when target batch size is 1–4, scheduler wake latency dominates; try micro-priming with many small requests to warm scheduler paths.
- Seed hygiene: RNG seeds affect arrival jitter and prompt choice; always record them in artifacts.

Artifacts to capture per run (minimum)
- loadbench config YAML (text)
- recorded seed list (text)
- priming snapshot file if used
- raw metrics JSON (latency histogram, token counts)
- nvml frequency & temp logs
- optional nsys profile for a representative 10s window

Example quick experiment matrix (30–90 minutes total)
1) Baseline: run mini-scale with default runtime flags, seeds 101/102/103 (15m total).
2) Patch A (scheduler tweak): run same config + patch (15m).
3) Patch B (batching window change): run same config + patch (15m).
4) Rehydrate baseline snapshot to confirm snapshot equivalence (10m).
5) Collate seeds and compute median p95/p99; if patch median deviates > 8% open INF ticket.

Open TODOs and followups
- Automate snapshot naming + metadata (who ran, git sha, model sha).
- Add a small dashboard that plots seed variance over time for quick triage.
- Validate micro-primer durations across MIG slices — might need slice-specific tuning.

Notes to self
- Keep prompt set small but representative; avoid heavy rare tokens that trigger different kernels.
- When in doubt about noise source, increase run length and repeat. Small runs are cheap but sometimes hide long-tail effects.

Appendix: quick primer checklist (copyable)
- [ ] Image sha recorded
- [ ] Model version recorded
- [ ] CUDA & driver recorded
- [ ] Seed list saved
- [ ] Priming snapshot created
- [ ] NVML & nsys logs captured
- [ ] 3 seeds completed

End of note. If this pattern looks useful we should bake it into the CI microbench pipeline so engineers can get fast signal before longer stability runs.
